output.headline: UK shares findings of damning climate crisis national security report suppressed under Starmer
output.standfirst: Ed Miliband tells foreign ministers from the EU, Kenya and other countries that the coming El Niño poses a critical threat to national defences
output.bodyHtml:
The UK has told countries around the world that the climate and nature crises, together with the coming El Niño, threaten their national security and defence, sharing the findings of a report that was suppressed under Keir Starmer.

Ed Miliband, the UK’s foreign secretary, presented the findings to foreign ministers from the EU, Kenya and other countries on Wednesday night, at a private meeting during the UN general assembly in New York, drawing on the report by the UK’s spy chiefs which found that the collapse of natural systems around the world would lead to conflict, migration and food shortages.

Miliband told the meeting, the first such discussion among foreign ministers, that the coming El Niño, supercharged by climate breakdown, would test the world’s food systems as never before.

“We face an El Niño that is already set to be the most intense in living memory,” he said. “This will intensify climate shocks that compound and cascade across borders, threatening food and water security, displacing communities, putting pressure on markets and scarring economies.”

This year’s heatwaves, bad harvests and food price inflation showed governments what lies ahead, he said, and must be addressed at the highest levels.

“Climate change and nature loss have never been issues for climate and environment ministers alone,” he said. “They are defining challenges for our citizens, our economies, our foreign policy and our national security.”

With the backing of Andy Burnham, the UK prime minister, Miliband set out research showing that the collapse of global ecosystems such as in the Amazon and Congo rainforests, driven by the climate crisis and the destruction of nature, would affect national security around the world.

The joint intelligence committee (JIC) report, revealed by the Guardian, had been due to be published last October, but was suppressed by Downing Street on the eve of its launch. A redacted version was issued in January under the Freedom of Information Act, though ministers have continued to resist calls for the full report to be made public.

Richard Nugee, a retired general and security expert, told the Guardian that governments should treat the climate as they would any other threat to national security, such as sabotage by hostile states.

“If a bridge is washed away, it has the same impact whether it’s done by [a foreign power] or the climate,” he said. “The climate crisis will affect food security, energy security, water security, and lead to migration and potentially the recruitment of farmers to [terrorist organisations such as] Isis. Countries should absolutely be treating this as a national security issue.”

He said it was unsurprising that the JIC report was suppressed and redacted, since it was “very rare” for security reports to be published.

Miliband is to appoint a new special representative for climate security, along with a new ministerial taskforce on “the national security and resilience risks of a changing climate and nature loss”, bringing together military and security experts with climate scientists.

He also announced £330m for the Global Environment Facility, the main international fund for protecting nature, which will go towards protecting forests, oceans and other critical ecosystems in developing countries.

The closed-door meeting among foreign ministers followed a public speech Miliband gave on Monday at the UN general assembly, which touched on the links between climate and national security. Soon after taking office in July, the former energy secretary told the Guardian he intended to put the climate at the heart of UK foreign policy.

On Wednesday night, Miliband said: “The countries fit for the future will be those that see climate and nature as intrinsic to economic and national security. Countries that anticipate risks and invest in resilience before crises hit.

“Countries that seize the incredible opportunities the clean energy transition presents. Countries that don’t just see the connections but act on them.”

He added: “That is why the UK is placing climate and nature security at the heart of our national security and foreign policy decision-making.”

Adrian Ramsay, the Green party MP for Waveney Valley, who has campaigned for the JIC report to be made public, said: “It’s good that the foreign secretary is presenting the findings of this crucial report to ministers from other governments.

“But it begs the question, why are MPs in this country still being denied access to the full report? And, most importantly, why has our government still not published its response to how it will address the stark findings?”
